title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — passiva Deo? originale; before GAR 2
pass_a_gloss: Next, if the man himself privates himself of justice, is this not enough that he be privated of justice? What need is there that after he has privated himself of justice God should deprive him of justice? for this privation must be later than that, if that is violation of the law, this the consequent penalty of that violation. Further I ask, privation of original justice as it was in Adam or is in us all — of what sort is the privation? if active, I have what I want: it is violation of the law, not however a penalty denounced by the law. If passive, it is not violation of the law, not sin, but only penalty. Which is to deny original sin. Finally, does Scripture anywhere teach that God privated Adam of justice? How then did the Learned Man dare to assert it? Certainly the reverence by which I am led toward God cannot let my conscience bear that assertion. For who privates a man of justice makes him unjust and is the cause of his injustice. Which even to suspect of God seems to me unlawful. But the Learned Man brings a second reply by which he takes away what he gave: let us hear it.
pass_b_english: Second: if the man has already stripped himself of righteousness, is that not enough for him to be without it? Why must God strip him again afterward? The divine stripping would have to come later than the self-stripping, if the latter is the law-breach and the former its following penalty. Third I ask what sort of privation original righteousness is, in Adam and in us. If active, I win: it is law-breaking, not a legally announced penalty. If only passive, it is neither law-breaking nor sin but bare penalty—and that denies original sin. Fourth: does any Scripture say God stripped Adam of righteousness? How then dare the learned man assert it? Reverence for God will not let my conscience bear that claim. Whoever strips a man of righteousness makes him unjust and causes his injustice—an idea I may not even entertain of God. But now he offers a second reply that retracts what he just gave; let us hear it.
source_text: Deinde si se homo ipse privat justitia, nonne hoc satis est ut sit justitia privatus? Quid opus est, ut postquam sese ipse privavit justitia, Deus eum privet justitia? oportet enim hanc privationem illa posteriorem esse, siquidem illa est violatio legis, haec illam violationem consequens poena. Praeterea, quaero, privatio justitiae originalis quatenus fuit in Adamo, aut est in nobis omnibus, qualis sit privatio? si est activa, habeo quod volo, est violatio legis, non autem poena lege denunciata. Si est passiva, non est violatio legis, non est peccatum, sed poena tantum. Id quod est negare peccatum originale. Denique, Docet-ne alicubi Scriptura Deum privasse Adamum justitia? Quomodo ergo ausus est Vir Doctus id asserere? Certe, qua ducor erga Deum reverentia, ferre non potest mea conscientia illam assertionem. Nam qui privat hominem justitia, facit eum injustum ejusque injustitiae causa est. Id quod vel suspicari de Deo mihi nefas esse videtur. Sed secundam affert Vir Doctus responsionem, qua tollit id quod dedit: eam audiamus.

choices.choice: Passive only = deny originale; Scripture silent on God privating
choices.why: Closes first PLAC reply before GAR 2
